scope: Official primary references; all worked financial numbers and graphs are synthetic illustrations, not market data.

claims: EV/EBITDA uses enterprise-value numerator and matching enterprise operating profit denominator; EBITDA is not FCFF.
P/S = P/E × profit margin with positive net earnings and matching periods.
Gordon DDM P0 = D1/(Ke-g) requires Ke>g; synthetic D1 2, Ke 8%, g 3% yields 40.
Exit terminal multiple requires comparable firm and valuation date; fifth-year EBITDA 150 at 8x gives TV 1200 discounted at WACC10% to 745.11.
High revenue growth is not the same as free cash flow growth; reinvestment and dilution matter.
Three-stage fictional model revenue0=100, growth20%, margin20%, tax25%, reinvest4% of revenue, WACC10%, terminal growth3%, EV=249.51 and discounted terminal share=84.2%.
PEGR and R-IRR intersection framework is a particular published research proposal, not a theorem invalidating general DCF.
Unit economics example (50-20)*1000-15000=15000 with break-even 500 units.
Indirect cash-flow bridge 120+20-35-25+15=95 before capital expenditures.
Research requires audit-traceable evidence, falsification criteria, and evidence-quality differentiation.
OHLC must satisfy high >= open and close and low <= open and close.
Two-for-one stock splits do not automatically imply a 50% holding loss.
Signals must be formed only after all necessary price data are available; false breakouts and data snooping matter.
SMA is trailing average, EMA uses alpha=2/(N+1).
MACD(12,26,9) line is EMA12 minus EMA26, signal EMA9(DIF), histogram DIF minus signal; some platforms multiply histogram by 2.
Wilder RSI uses gains and losses initialized over 14 intervals then recursively smoothed; average gain1.5 and loss0.5 imply RSI75.
Two-asset volatility equals sqrt(wA²sigmaA²+wB²sigmaB²+2wAwB rho sigmaA sigmaB).
Two equal 20%-sigma assets at equal weights and rho0 produce 14.14% volatility, rho1=20%, rho-1=0% idealized.
CAPM is a conditional equilibrium pricing model; with Rf3%, market premium6%, beta1.2 implies expected 10.2%.
Efficient frontier relies on estimated means, covariances and constraints; empirical alpha is model-specific.

CFA 2026 Portfolio Risk and Return II

claims: NBS PMI is monthly diffusion index with expansion-contraction threshold 50; not GDP growth.
Monetary transmission can affect safe yields, risk premia and expected cash flow differently.
Exact Fisher real rate formula for nominal 5%, inflation 2% yields 2.94%.
GICS is a taxonomy with 11 broad sectors, classification evolves over time.
Porter five forces explain profit competition between suppliers, buyers, entrants, substitutes and incumbents.
Unit-economics math assumes price 100, variable cost 65, fixed cost 20000, volume 1000; synthetic.
FCFF/WACC corresponds to firm value; FCFE/cost of equity corresponds to equity value.
Synthetic 5-year FCFF [100,110,120,130,140], WACC 10%, stable g 3% yields EV about 1726.79 and TV PV share about 74.07%.
Gordon terminal value requires WACC>g and reinvestment and growth assumptions must be consistent.
P/E, P/B, PEG require positive and consistent denominators; a negative P/E lacks standard cheapness meaning.
Steady-state justified P/B formula (ROE-g)/(Ke-g) assumes clean surplus and sustainable reinvestment.
PB = PE × ROE only with exactly matched book denominator and equity/earnings scope.
VaR is a loss-distribution quantile for a given confidence level and horizon, not a maximum loss; parameter method VaR = mu - z*sigma.
CVaR (expected shortfall) is the average loss beyond VaR and is subadditive; the Basel market-risk framework uses expected shortfall rather than VaR for internal models.
Recovery gain after a drawdown d is 1/(1-d)-1, so -20% needs +25%, -50% needs +100%, -80% needs +400%.
Kelly fraction f*=(bp-q)/b; with p=0.60 and b=2 it is 0.40, and half-Kelly is 0.20.
Synthetic teaching example (construct, not data): 95% VaR 3.1% with conditional tail average 4.8%.
Prospect theory values outcomes relative to a reference point with a steeper loss side; Kahneman and Tversky (1979) median estimates are alpha=beta~0.88 and lambda~2.25.
Constructed example (teaching): x=1000 gives v(+)=~436.5 and v(-)=~982.2; the ratio is the lambda parameter, not a measured psychological constant.
Disposition effect (selling winners and holding losers) is documented empirically by Odean (1998).
Barber and Odean (2001) report higher trading frequency among men and an association between over-trading and lower net returns.
Sentiment indicators (margin balance, turnover, futures basis, volatility index) are descriptive and do not imply reversal timing.
Graham number = sqrt(22.5*EPS*BVPS); with EPS=3 and BVPS=20 it is ~36.74 and the two-thirds buy limit is ~24.49. It is a screening rule, not intrinsic value.
Buffett's shift from Graham cigar-butts to quality businesses at fair prices adds a moat, and with it the risk of a simultaneous earnings and multiple decline.
Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) documented momentum returns in the US; multiple studies report stronger short-horizon reversal in China's A-share market, and these results are sample dependent.
Reflexivity (Soros) is an interpretive framework, not a directly testable formula; it must be reduced to observable funding conditions to be tested.
sources: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis; Graham, The Intelligent Investor
Fisher, Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits

claims: Factor decomposition: r_i = alpha_i + beta_i*r_mkt + sum_k beta_ik*f_k + epsilon_i.
Backtest pitfalls: survivorship bias, look-ahead bias, data snooping and parameter overfitting.
Standardization z=(x-mean)/std; with value=15, mean=20, std=5 it is -1.00.
Synthetic overfitting illustration: in-sample error falls monotonically while out-of-sample error is U-shaped in model complexity.
Real-world gaps: commissions, taxes, slippage, liquidity limits and capacity; the 'discount the Sharpe ratio' rule is not sourced and is not asserted.
sources: Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado & Zhu 2014, Notices of the AMS

claims: Factor construction workflow: winsorize, neutralize (industry and size), standardize, then combine.
ICIR = mean(IC)/std(IC); a synthetic 12-month IC series gives mean~0.0208, sd~0.0287 and ICIR~0.73 (construct, not measured).
Factor crowding can produce factor crashes when many strategies hold the same names; crowding measures are descriptive.
Factor timing is contested in the literature; this chapter does not claim any timing method is proven effective.
IC thresholds such as 0.03 are sample dependent and are not presented as standards.
sources: Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen 2013, Journal of Finance

claims: Frontier factors are treated as hypotheses: with hundreds of tested candidates, a t threshold near 2 is too weak; Harvey-Liu-Zhu suggest roughly 3.
R&D factor RD/MV or RD/Sales quantifies expensed investment; comparisons require consistent capitalization and disclosure coverage; input is not output (Hirshleifer-Hsu-Li use innovation efficiency).
Performance-persistence (reverse-valuation) construction: industry mean PE +/- k standard deviations defines a fair price band; loses meaning for loss-making firms.
Fund-flow factors come from transaction data and decay quickly; turnover and trading costs can consume the gross alpha (Novy-Marx & Velikov).
Analyst factors: revisions matter more than levels; coverage and optimism biases must be removed.
Industry-rotation factorization moves industry bets into a stock-level score and distributes concentration risk.
Teaching numbers on this page are constructed (RD/Sales example, fair PE band, t~2.51); no real factor performance is cited.
sources: Harvey, Liu & Zhu 2016, Review of Financial Studies
Hou, Xue & Zhang 2015, Review of Financial Studies
Fama & French 2015, Journal of Financial Economics

claims: Cross-industry PE comparison is misleading; PB-ROE matrix places each industry on profitability and valuation axes.
Identity PB = PE x ROE (same period/definition) gives implied PE = PB / ROE. Constructed examples: bank PB0.6/ROE10% -> PE6; semiconductor PB8/ROE15% -> PE ~53.
The definition of '景气' evolves (high ROE -> high G -> delta-g); presented as an interpretive framework, not a fact list.
Multi-signal sector scoring reduces single-signal noise; weights must be validated out of sample. No brokerage framework or backtest numbers cited.
Rotation methods (momentum, reversal, fundamental) each fit specific regimes; no performance figures are given.
Crowding filter: trigger at top decile, action below benchmark, release below 70th percentile; risk management not reversal prediction.
sources: Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen 2013, Journal of Finance
Fama & French 2015, Journal of Financial Economics

claims: Data sources fall into three tiers (professional terminals, open Python endpoints, overseas); no product prices are given.
Price adjustment: forward-adjusted for backtests, backward-adjusted for long-run cumulative return, unadjusted only for very short horizons.
Ex-rights reference price = (prev close - cash dividend + rights price x rights ratio) / (1 + stock-dividend ratio + rights ratio); constructed example 20, div0.5, 10-for-5 -> 13.0.
Look-ahead bias arises when financial data is matched to reporting period instead of disclosure date; align by disclosure date.
Consolidated vs parent-only statements and CAS vs IFRS differences must be reconciled before cross-market comparison.
Cleaning: remove ST/delisted and newly listed samples, forward-fill low-missing series, align frequencies to a common timestamp.
Local database should store data version and update timestamps because adjusted history can be revised.
Python is a low-cost starting point for personal/teaching quant; claims about 'market share' or package counts are avoided as they are unsourced and time-varying.
Panel operations: groupby before shift/rolling/pct_change; shifting before grouping leaks across instruments.
TA-Lib expects NumPy arrays and has indicator warm-up (e.g., 14-day RSI has 13 missing leading values).
Backtest skeleton: signal generation -> portfolio construction -> evaluation; signal lagged by shift(1) to avoid look-ahead.
Vectorized vs event-driven backtests; credibility depends on modeling cost, tradability and timing, not on the framework.
Cost estimate: annual cost ~ turnover x 2 x one-way cost; constructed example 50 x 2 x 0.1% = 10%/yr.
Backtest vs live gap comes from unmodeled frictions: latency, rejected orders, limit-up/down and suspension, quote delay, fee changes, ex-rights cash.
The gap is not signed: live can be better or worse depending on whether frictions are costs or benefits; list them instead of applying a blanket haircut.

Program-trading regulation (China) covers high-frequency monitoring, a reporting regime and possible traffic fees; the page states the framework direction, not the exact text, and requires checking current CSRC/exchange rules.
Stamp duty and commission rates must be checked for their current effective value; the historical rate is not presented as current.
Round-trip cost ~ 2 x commission + stamp duty + 2 x slippage; constructed example 0.025/0.05/0.05 -> 0.20%; no impact cost included.
Live risk control has three layers: hard real-time limits, alerting, and post-close review; risk control protects you, it does not predict.

claims: ML can fit history well; danger is fitting a specific regime, not insufficient accuracy. Three causes: overfitting/data-snooping, regime shift, label/feature leakage.
LLM factor-mining loop (generate-evaluate-evolve) is genetic programming; it amplifies multiple testing, so an independent out-of-sample + multiplicity gate is required.
No architecture dominates across regimes; financial data has low signal-to-noise, so deep learning overfits more easily than in vision/language.
Regime shift: train across full bull-bear cycles, use confidence thresholds to de-risk, keep human override.
Unstructured text: domain-fine-tuned sentiment models and text-as-representation (VTA) research direction; look-ahead, coverage/survivorship, and nonlinearity are traps.
Metrics: precision = TP/(TP+FP), recall = TP/(TP+FN), F1 harmonic mean; constructed example TP30/FP70/FN20 -> precision 30%, recall 60%, F1 ~40%.
No institutional AI stock-picking performance, accuracy or IC numbers are cited on this page.
sources: Gu, Kelly & Xiu 2020, Review of Financial Studies
Harvey, Liu & Zhu 2016, Review of Financial Studies

limitations: All figures and calculations are original synthetic illustrations, not market price or forecasts.
Automated static structural and browser QA checks do not replace external link freshness and factual review.
Financial reporting and market-specific trading rules must be reverified as they evolve.
Chapters 11–15: derived indicators are features, not tested forecasts; constructed valuation and covariance matrices are hypothetical.
